newsitem.title: RUSSIA: Recovering Yeltsin much more active, Kremlin says.
newsitem.headline: Recovering Yeltsin much more active, Kremlin says.

text.p: President Boris Yeltsin, who is recovering from pneumonia, was more active on Sunday and has begun working in his hospital room, the Kremlin said.
The latest report by doctors who examined the 65-year-old leader on Sunday morning said he was in a stable condition with normal blood pressure, pulse and temperature.
"To a significant degree, his activity has increased, and B.N. Yeltsin has begun to work on documents," the bulletin said.
Yeltsin checked into Moscow's elite Central Clinical Hospital on Wednesday with pneumonia in both lungs, just two months after undergoing quintuple heart bypass surgery.
Pneumonia, a serious infection or inflammation of the lungs, can affect one or both lungs. An infection of both lungs is considered more serious and difficult to treat.

There was no word on what papers the president was working on. The only document released by the Kremlin on Sunday in Yeltsin's name was a salutation to the people of Karachayevo-Cherkessia, congratulating them on the 75th anniversary of their semi-autnomous North Caucasus region.

Chief Kremlin doctor Sergei Mironov said on Friday he expects Yeltsin to leave the hospital early this coming week and then continue his recovery for about three weeks. The president is receiving antibiotics to combat the pneumonia, doctors say.

The president's continued absence from the Kremlin has raised fears that the man who once symbolised the vigour of the new democratic Russia will not have enough energy to solve the country's persistent and manifold problems.
The president's latest bout of ill health has also opened up a debate on whether Russia should alter its constitution to shift power from the president to the legislature.
At least one Moscow daily newspaper suggested on Saturday that, because of his prolonged illnesses, it might be time for Yeltsin, post-Soviet Russia's first president, to step down.
"Regretfully, it is obvious that the president has no strength left to attend to affairs of state properly," the liberal daily Komsomolskaya Pravda said on Saturday.
Other newspapers have expressed doubts over the government's ability to move forward under the leadership of a sick man.
On Sunday, however, the mass-circulation Moskovsky Komsomolets said the government has been working effectively without Yeltsin's participation.

"For the last half year, both the country and bureaucrats have got used to the participation in name only of the head of state in the country's affairs," it wrote in a front-page story. "The mechanism of taking decisions has been well-tuned since the time of his absence from the Kremlin."
Some of Yeltsin's opponents have, however, seized upon his latest illness to call for his resignation.
His former security chief Alexander Lebed has called for him to quit, and Communist Party leader Gennady Zyuganov has insisted for months that a sick Yeltsin was incapable of ruling the country.
Average Russians, many of whom see little direct connection between their daily lives and what happens in the Kremlin, appeared calmer about Yeltsin's latest illness.
Financial markets also shrugged off reports on his health, sending Russian markets into record territory on Friday. Some analysts said they expected more enthusiastic buying on Monday.

Mironov predicted the president would "ideally" be able to resume full-time activities in the Kremlin after January 25 to 27. "I'm sure there will be no 50-50 situation -- the president spending half the time in the Kremlin and half in hospital," Mironov said in a television interview broadcast on Saturday.
Another issue Yeltsin may face after his recovery are calls to change the constitution.
The chairman of parliament's upper house said on Friday it was time to consider amending the 1993 constitution, drawn up after Yeltsin used tanks to put down a rebellion by parliament.
The communists, the largest group in parliament, also say they favour changes that would give legislators more power.
